Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
This paper presents a series of experiments testing different hypotheses about how the
presence of feedback might affect risky choice behavior. Strikingly, the experiments quite
consistently speak against feedback-dependent learning, the dominant account in the
literature. Specifically, differences between feedback and no-feedback conditions are already
present before any feedback is experienced. Moreover, trial-by-trial analyses indicate that
participants rather become less (vs. more) likely to choose a risky option after experiencing its
most desirable outcome. The authors interpret these findings as pointing towards mechanisms
of anticipatory regret and/or epistemic curiosity.
The experiments are meticulously designed to provide diagnostic tests pitting different
candidate hypotheses regarding the effects of feedback against each other. Thereby, they
allow the authors to fill in some quite striking but thus far overlooked blind-spots in the
literature, which existed because factors such as risk and EV were typically not fully
orthogonalized in prior work. Moreover, the behavioral results are highly consistent across the
different reported experiments and also analyses of existing data, speaking towards the
robustness of the findings. Although overall, this is already an excellent manuscript, I do
have a few questions and comments that should be addressed in a revision (see details below).
R3.0
We thank the reviewer for this very positive appreciation of our work.
1. From a conceptual stance, it may be problematic to characterize the present findings as
“dispositional“ changes in risk preference. After all, ”dispositional“ seems to imply that these
effects might be long-lasting over time and/or concern a relatively stable disposition to
take/avoid risks. Given such an interpretation of the term, one would maybe expect the effects
of feedback on one block to carry over to subsequent blocks—potentially even to blocks
without feedback. However, this intuitive interpretation of the term does not seem to be what
the authors mean to refer to here. It rather seems that the reported choice patterns are adapted
from block to block to the currently experienced task structure, rather than reflecting
”dispositional“ changes in risk preference. Thus, changing the terminology might be advisable.
Though ”merely“ concerning terminology, this point seems important to address, in the light of
recent discussions in the risky choice literature about whether risk preference is indeed a
stable disposition, and whether this disposition can even be measured using behavioral tasks.
R3.1
We thank the reviewer for this remark and note that Reviewer 2 expressed a very similar
concern (see R2.1). We agree that terminology is important. After careful consideration and
consultation with a native English speaker, we concluded that "attitudinal" is a more
appropriate adjective for the effect we are describing, as "attitude" refers to more malleable
states, rather than stable traits (see the phrase “change of attitude”).
2. The authors highlight that anticipated regret should affect complete feedback decisions. Do
they mean it should *exclusively* play a role given complete feedback? After all, it seems that
anticipated regret might also arise in partial feedback situations where the participant
considers choosing the risky option, but anticipates that the lower outcome might be obtained.
Here it is possible to experience (or anticipate) regret, even without feedback about the safe
option, because the realized outcome of the safe option can be inferred with certainty.
Therefore, I wonder, to what extent might anticipated regret explain behavior in the partial
feedback conditions? (How) can one disentangle this type of anticipatory regret from
epistemic curiosity here? Could the authors please present additional analyses to assess the
relative contribution of anticipatory regret and epistemic curiosity in the partial feedback conditions?
R3.2
The Reviewer raises a valid point regarding the possibility that anticipated regret may shape
risk preferences even in partial feedback situations. We acknowledge that this perspective
aligns with prominent decision theory models that attribute a role to counterfactual emotions,
such as regret and disappointment, in description-based choices, even in the absence of
feedback (see for example seminal work by Loomes et al22).
That said, based on our data, we do not have evidence to support the presence of regret in
the partial feedback condition. Indeed, in our design, anticipated or experienced regret should
induce a monotonic increase in the probability of choosing the risky option as a function of the
probability of the maximum outcome for that option (see additional information in R1.1 for a
fuller explanation). This monotonic relationship is key for detecting (or disentangling) the
influence of regret on risk preferences.
With this diagnostic pattern in mind, we examined our data to see if the influence of regret on
risk preferences can be detected in other conditions (even if below a significant threshold).
Following the reviewer’s suggestion, we focused on:
1. The "No feedback" conditions present in both the partial and complete feedback
experiments.
2. The "Partial feedback" condition.
As illustrated in Rebuttal Figure 9 (below), a closer examination of these cases provides no
evidence for the influence of regret. In fact, in the "No feedback" conditions (Case 1) and in
the "Partial feedback" condition, we observed a non-significant trend in the opposite
direction—a decrease rather than an increase. Therefore, while it is theoretically possible, as
the reviewer suggests, that anticipated regret could have influenced choices in the conditions
without feedback or with partial feedback (potentially based on mental simulations of possible
outcomes), the data indicate otherwise.
This aigns with the consensual idea23 that regret is, fundamentally, a comparison between
obtained and forgone outcomes, and this comparison, as well as the anticipation of it, is more
salient in the complete feedback condition. Thus, it is not surprising that, while theoretically
possible, we did not observe evidence of regret in the remaining conditions (no feedback or
partial feedback), where outcome comparisons are not made explicit. Finally, while we are not
aware of any study examining the intensity of regret as a function of the saliency of outcomes’
comparison, it is worth mentioning that complete feedback has been shown to intensify the
impact of regret compared to when partial 24 or no 1 feedback is provided, as well as that
experience (namely, exposure to feedback) increases sensitivity to regret 1,25.

3. The author’s notion that learning should generally increase EV maximization rests on the
assumption that the process of learning itself adheres to a normative standard. However, there
are experiments, for instance in the realm of Bayesian updating, that have demonstrated that
people do not necessarily integrate new information in an optimal manner. Instead, they
sometimes over- or under-adjust their expectations in the light of new information. In this light,
can one really argue that learning should *generally* render choice behavior more optimal?
R3.3
The Reviewer is absolutely correct; there is ample evidence of biased reinforcement learning
and Bayesian integration (including in our own studies). We have revised our paper to clarify
what we believe are the predictions of the learning hypothesis. In light of this comment, we
have further qualified our claim that learning should increase maximization in both the
introduction and the discussion.
We also take this opportunity to emphasize that the absence of a beneficial effect of feedback
on maximization is not the only result that challenges the learning hypothesis. Specifically, the
learning hypothesis is contradicted by the first trial effect—the observation that the effect is
present before any feedback is experienced, implying that it is not mediated by experienced
feedback. Furthermore, the learning hypothesis is challenged by our trial-by-trial analysis,
which shows that participants exhibit a "negative recency effect," meaning they tend to not
repeat rewarded risky choices. Crucially, no learning process, however biased, would predict
this outcome.
We have copied below the relevant sections of the amended introduction and discussion:
We shall refer to this category of accounts as the learning hypothesis. Because the
integration of feedback in future choices is supposed to correct originally distorted
subjective probabilities, the learning hypothesis often assumes that the presence of
feedback should correct representational biases and, as a consequence, promote
optimal (i.e., expected value maximizing) choices 26–28. Admittedly, though, these
simple predictions from the learning hypothesis can be challenged, e.g., by the
presence of learning biases 29,30, or when the probabilities of the outcomes are extreme
and the options are not sufficiently sampled: two conditions that lead the experienced
and the actual frequency of the outcomes to diverge31.
[…]
Critically, in contrast to the learning hypothesis, which supposes that the effect of the
feedback should emerge gradually, the attitudinal hypothesis conceives that it can
emerge even before any feedback is experienced – i.e., by anticipation. Because the
two hypotheses differ in the temporal relation with respect to the time of choice and
outcomes, fine-grained temporal dynamics can dissociate the two accounts: attitudinal
effects precede choices while learning effects follow outcomes. In addition, the two
hypotheses are also different in their relation to choice optimality. Learning
mechanisms are generally supposed to correct representational biases and,
accordingly, should increase expected value maximization. Attitudinal ones are more
silent in that respect.
4. Did the emergence of the abrupt effect of feedback after the first trial depend on which
option was chosen on the first trial, and on which feedback was received? Arguably, under
learning, the direction of the effect should probably depend on these factors. If there is an
invariable increase in risk taking, this would provide further evidence against learning.
R3.4
We thank the reviewer for this valuable insight and suggestion. Indeed, we lacked a proper
characterization of the abrupt emergence of the feedback effect on the second trial in the

Importantly, as the reviewer suggested, this analysis further supports an attitudinal change
mechanism and challenges the learning hypothesis. Since the effect is present in the second

Figure R10 A&C), and additively to the main effect of the previous choice type on R-rates
(Figure R10 B&D).
We believe this result is important, so we have mention it in the results section of the main text

A follow-up question is whether the abrupt emergence of the feedback effect on the
second trial in the experiments without block instructions was dependent on the choice
made on the first trial. We observe that the main effect of feedback is observed
regardless of the previous choice type (sure/safe, versus risky), and additively to the
main effect of the previous choice type on R-rates (Figure 5A and 5C). Since the
second-trial effect is present regardless of the choice made on the first trial, only the
mere discovery of the presence of feedback (and consequent attitudinal change) could

Next, we wanted to check whether the abrupt effect of feedback between the first and
the second trial in experiments without block instructions was influenced by the

nature of the outcome received on the first trial (Figure 5B and 5D). This result further

5. Regarding p.15, Figure 3. In Experiments 3-4, the R-rate is below .5, even in the p=50
condition. It seems that under anticipated regret, as presented by the authors, one would
expect an R-rate of pretty much exactly 50% here, because the safe and the risky option each

condition). How can one explain that this does not seem to be the case in the data?
R3.5
We thank the reviewer for allowing us to clarify this point. The reviewer's observation regarding
the p=50 condition (“under anticipated regret, as presented by the authors, one would expect
an R-rate of pretty much exactly 50%”) would be correct if one assumed that regret is the sole
determinant of risk preference. However, we believe that feedback-induced adherence to
regret influences risk preferences on top of pre-existing tendencies, which can be adequately
captured by standard models of risk aversion. To put it another way, we refer to regret to
explain relative differences on R-rates, rather than their absolute levels.
We believe this point is made even clearer in the revised manuscript, where we have
expanded the explanation concerning the role of regret and how it is computationally captured
in standard models such as the BEAST (see R1.1).
6. It is quite surprising that the authors find no differences between gain and loss conditions
in Experiment 7. People seem to behave slightly risk-averse in the no-feedback condition and
risk-neutral in the feedback condition, regardless of domain (gain/loss). How can these
findings be reconciled with many findings in the risky choice literature indicating that
preference patterns typically reverse between domains (the reflection effect)?
R3.6
We agree with the Reviewer that differences in risk preference between the gains and losses
domains (Exp 7) could be anticipated based on what is known about loss aversion and the
consequent “reflection effect. Despite the robustness of the reflection effect in many contexts,
it is also worth pointing out that the traditional demonstration of loss aversion and reflection
effect emerged from one-shot paradigms; therefore, we can also consider that choice
repetition and the presence of feedback are additional experimental factors that may blunt or
undermine the detection of them. In line with this, we found that E2017 reported only a weak
replication of the reflection effect in the “no feedback” condition and no effect—or even a
reversed reflection effect—in the “feedback” condition.
Furthermore, a closer look at the literature suggests that loss aversion—and, consequently,
the reflection effect—may not be as generalizable as originally proposed. Specifically, we refer
to a few insightful studies led by Eldad Yechiam, which propose that loss aversion tends to
materialize with larger losses rather than smaller ones. Given that our experiment involved
payoffs in the range of only a few euros, it is plausible that we fall within this specific
circumstance.
We have mentioned these arguments in the supplementary discussion dedicated to
Experiment 7’s results:
In our Experiment, we found no evidence of the reflection effect, which should translate
into higher risk seeking in the loss, compared to the gain domain. This may appear
surprising, as the reflection effect is traditionally attributed to loss aversion, which, in
turn, is generally considered a robust feature of human decision-making32. Our findings
become less surprising when one notices that the traditional demonstration of the
reflection effect has been made in one-shot paradigms33. In contrast, in paradigms with
choice repetition and/or feedback (namely, paradigms closer to ours) the reflection
effect is much less robust or even reversed (Erev et al., 2017 reported only a weak
replication of the reflection effect in the “no feedback” condition and no effect—or even
a reversed reflection effect—in the “feedback” condition; Rigoli et al., 2019 report
null/reversed results of risk attitudes as a function of decision domain too). Related to
the reflection effect, loss aversion has also been shown to have been overstated, as it
seems to be present only for very large losses and only in a fraction of studies that
report it35.
7. The analysis of trial-by-trial changes in behavior (p.19 f.) indicates that people adapt their
behavior to feedback in a way reminiscent of a gambler’s fallacy. That is, indeed, some
feedback-dependent adaptation of behavior on the trial-level seems to be present in the data.
Because this adaptation seems to be based on a misconstrued notion of non-independent
outcomes (i.e., gambler’s fallacy), the finding may speak against learning in the sense of
moving closer to optimal behavior, and this is also the key inference the authors draw.
However, the mere fact that such trial-by-trial effects exist also indicates that „dispositional“
changes alone are insufficient to fully explain the consequences of feedback. This should be
mentioned and discussed.
